paragraphs.text: Quando rebellabat Sheba, saith the Syriac, made upon the occasion of Sheba’s rebellion presently after Absalom’s. Hence he cries out, as one almost overwhelmed,
paragraphs.anchor: A Psalm of David

paragraphs.text: Thou, who delightest to save such as are forsaken of their hopes. The Fathers generally take this psalm to be prophetic touching the passion of Christ, and his praying then to the Father. David had his troubles which gave occasion to the penning of this psalm, but those were all but as a picture and prelude of Christ’s far greater sorrows, Spiritus autem sanctus manifeste se prodit in hoc psalmo.
paragraphs.anchor: Save me, O God

paragraphs.text: Ever after Noah’s flood, that dismal destruction, great and grievous afflictions were set forth by the rushing in of waters, and overwhelming therewith. God’swrath was poured upon Christ as a mighty torrent of waters, and, therefore, this expression applied to him hath a special emphasis; his soul was heavy even to the death. Fluctus fluctum trudebat, One deep called upon another, &c. Oh the soul of sufferings which his soul then suffered!
paragraphs.anchor: For the waters are come in unto my soul

paragraphs.text: Heb. in the mire of depth, or gulf, as Babylon was afterwards called, Isa 44:27. Here he stuck, and under water, and so must perish, if he had not present help.
paragraphs.anchor: I sink in deep mire

paragraphs.text: As a drowning man, while he can be heard, crieth for help.
paragraphs.anchor: I am weary of mg crying

paragraphs.text: Or, parched, raucitate laborant fauces.
paragraphs.anchor: My throat is dried

paragraphs.text: With much weeping and long looking. This is a piece of the curse, Lev 26:16. Christ became a curse for us, Gal 3:13.
paragraphs.anchor: Mine eyes fail

paragraphs.text: Christ, besides his inward fears and griefs caused by the sense of his Father’s wrath for our sins, was set against and assaulted both by men and devils (in that three hours’ darkness especially) with utmost might and malice.
paragraphs.anchor: They that hate me without a cause, &c.

paragraphs.text: Quod non rapui reddebam. David was dealt with as a felon or false dealer. Christ also was crucified for saying that he was the Son of God, Joh 19:7, though he held it no robbery to be equal with God, Php 2:6. The martyrs likewise were loaden with many calumnies and false criminations, that they might seem to suffer not as martyrs, but as malefactors.
paragraphs.anchor: Then I restored that which I took not away.

paragraphs.text: Secundum dici, non secundum esse; ironica enim est locutio. Thou knowest mine innocence, and how free I am of that folly, and those foul faults, wherewith they falsely charge me.
paragraphs.anchor: O God, thou knowest my foolishness

paragraphs.text: Let not them … be ashamed for my sake] Give me not up to passions of dishonour, to opprobrious practices, whereby religion might be reproached, or good people reviled and abused, much less staggered and set at a stand by my sufferings.

Whatever mine enemies pretend, they strike at thee, Lord, through my sides; and for thy sake alone it is that I am so bespattled, that I am even ashamed to look any one in the face. The most innocent may, upon the fulness of an aspersion, be put out of countenance.
paragraphs.anchor: Because for thy sake I have borne reproach

paragraphs.text: No otherwise than as if I were a mamzer (so the Hebrews call a bastard), that is, a strange blot to the family. Christ came to his own, but they received him not; yea, his own brethren believed not on him, Joh 7:5 This, when the Turks read in our Gospel, they wonder; and the Jews, therefore, slander his miracles, for not so manifest as we conceive.
paragraphs.anchor: I am become a stranger unto my brethren

paragraphs.text: Non amat qui non zelat. David’s love to God (much less the Lord Christ’s) would not suffer him to bear with God’s dishonour and the contempt of his ordinances. And this was it that procured him so much ill-will, and such a general alienation from nearest friends and allies.
paragraphs.anchor: For the zeal of thine house hath eaten me up

paragraphs.text: Wicked men soon set their mouths against heaven, and fall foul upon God himself. This David (and the Son of David) could not endure, nec aliter amare didicit, as Basil once answered those that blamed him for appearing so far for his friend, to his own great danger (Chrysost. lib. 2, de Sacerdot.).
paragraphs.anchor: And the reproaches of them that reproached thee

paragraphs.text: That I might thereby beat down my body, and tame that rebel flesh of mine.
paragraphs.anchor: When I wept, and chastened my soul with fasting

paragraphs.text: They said I did it in hypocrisy and design. So they dealt by the Baptist, that crucifix of mortification, Luk 7:33.
paragraphs.anchor: That was to my reproach

paragraphs.text: A fashion at solemn fasts among the Easterlings; as if they thought the coarsest clothing too good for them; and but for shame would have gone stark naked.
paragraphs.anchor: I made sackcloth also my garment

paragraphs.text: Dicterium. They would say, with mocking Michal, "How glorious was the king of Israel today, as one of the vain fellows!" 2Sa 6:20.
paragraphs.anchor: I became a proverb to them

paragraphs.text: Men of authority and dignity, who should have showed more grace and gravity. The saints are sure of enemies of all sorts. David was traduced at public and private meetings, seriis et ludicris, sobriis et ebriis.
paragraphs.anchor: They that sit in the gate

paragraphs.text: Heb. of the drinkers of strong drink; the ale stakes made ballads on their ale bench, de macie mea et miseria. These servants tear and toss my name, as curs do carrion.
paragraphs.anchor: And I was the song of the drunkards

paragraphs.text: So St Paul, "Being defamed," saith he, "we pray." Christ in like case committed himself to God in well-doing, 1Pe 2:15
paragraphs.anchor: But as for me, my prayer is unto thee, O Lord

paragraphs.text: Or, there will be an acceptable time.
paragraphs.anchor: In an acceptable time

paragraphs.text: Flebile principium melior fortuna sequetur.

i.e. De civitate Gehennae, from the state of hell, saith the Hebrew scholiast; {a} out of that deadly danger whereof he had complained, Psa 69:2. Alphonsus, king of Arragon, by a gracious condescension, helped a laden ass out of the mire with his own hand, and is renowned for it in history (Val. Max. Christ. 41). God helpeth his out full oft, and little notice is taken of it.
paragraphs.anchor: Deliver me out of the mire

paragraphs.text: {a} One who writes explanatory notes upon an author; esp. an ancient commentator upon a classical writer.
See Psa 69:1.
paragraphs.anchor: Let not the waterflood overflow me

paragraphs.text: Leave me not helpless and hopeless.
paragraphs.anchor: Let not the pit shut

paragraphs.text: Vivere spe facias qui moriturus eram.
It is not like the winter sun, that lighteth but heateth not; it is like the summer sun, that doth both.
paragraphs.anchor: Hear me, O Lord, for thy lovingkindness is good

paragraphs.text: Who am devoted to thy fear, and do, therefore, implore and expect thy favour.
paragraphs.anchor: And hide not thy face from thy servant

paragraphs.text: And so a fit object of thy pity.
paragraphs.anchor: For I am in trouble

paragraphs.text: Who seemest to be afar off; so the flesh suggesteth when help is any whit deferred.
paragraphs.anchor: Draw nigh unto my soul

paragraphs.text: Who else will excessively insult.
paragraphs.anchor: Because of mine enemies

paragraphs.text: That is enough for David, that God taketh cognizance of the injuries and indignities cast upon him; for he will surely right him.
paragraphs.anchor: Thou hast known my reproach

paragraphs.text: He knew his own innocence, and yet it much grieved him to be so defamed; for he knew that a good man should be as much as might be not only without fault, but without suspicion of a fault, as Augustus Caesar was wont to say of his house. Howsoever, it is happy that a true Christian hath always his cordial by him, 2Co 1:12. Our rejoicing is this, the testimony of our conscience.
paragraphs.anchor: Reproach hath broken mine heart, &c.

paragraphs.text: Heb. to lament with me, or to shake the head over me as mourners use to do, to run to my comfort, and to condole with me. David’s friends failed him in this office also. But that was not all.
paragraphs.anchor: And I looked for some to take pity

paragraphs.text: Venenum vel eicutam; and so showed themselves miserable comforters.
paragraphs.anchor: They gave me also gall for my meat

paragraphs.text: This befell David in figure, but Christ in the letter, Mat 27:34. It were happy if the vinegar given him might melt our adamantine hearts into godly sorrow.
paragraphs.anchor: And in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink

paragraphs.text: Let them eat their bane, and drink their poison; while all their cares are sauced with the wrath of God: Quoniam hoe mode cibarunt me, saith Kimchi, because they have served me on this sort. By "table," saith another interpreter, we are to understand all means of comfort and refreshing, both of body and soul, which turn to the ruin of the wicked, even an odour of death unto death, 2Co 2:15-16.
paragraphs.anchor: Let their table become a snare before them

paragraphs.text: Tremellius rendereth it, Pro retributionibus, pro tendicula ipsis, for recompenses, for a trap to them Rom 11:9; others, Pacifiea in rete! others again, Et ubi pacem sperant, illic impingant, Where they hope for peace let them fall.
paragraphs.anchor: And that which should have been, &c.

paragraphs.text: Let them be infatuated and besotted, that they may go hoodwinked to hell.
paragraphs.anchor: Let their eyes be darkened

paragraphs.text: Ne fugiant, saith R. Obadiah Gaon, that they may not be able to fly, or otherwise to help themselves; for in the loins and reins of a man lieth his strength, Deu 33:11. The Syriac hath it, Lumbi eorum sint curvi, viz. under their enemies’ burdens. See Rom 11:10, bow down their backs.
paragraphs.anchor: And make their loins continually to shake

paragraphs.text: By indignation, saith Basil, we are to understand speedy vengeance; by wrath, durable. This is befallen the nation of the Jews to the utmost, 1Th 2:14-16, or to the end, as some render it.
paragraphs.anchor: Pour out thine indignation upon them

paragraphs.text: Heb. their palaces, or castles, so named of being fair and high built, in row and order. It is here put not only for their habitation, but for their function. See Act 1:20.
paragraphs.anchor: Let their habitation be desolate

paragraphs.text: Lege et luge, Read and lament, saith one, speaking of the ruin of Jerusalem by the Romans, under Vespasian, and again under Hadrian, by whom all Judaea was left almost uninhabited, the Jews utterly banished, and forbidden upon pain of death to look toward their own country (Dio in Hadrian). At this day there be not to be found in Jerusalem itself a hundred households of Jews. Behold the severity of God for the contempt of Christ and his people (Breerwood’s Enquirer).
paragraphs.anchor: And let none dwell in their tents

paragraphs.text: Christ was "stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted," Isa 53:4. Him they persecuted to the death, and abused, when he was at the greatest under, with bitter taunts and Satanical sarcasms; so the pagans and Papists dealt by the dying martyrs; and so profane persons and malicious miscreants do still by God’s poor afflicted; falling as cursed curs upon the dog that is worried; and as when a deer is shot the rest of the herd push him out of their company: so here. Now, if it could be said of Mithridates, that he hated such as maliciously persecuted virtue forsaken of fortune; much more may we think doth God abhor such cruel criminals as are here spoken of. See Isa 47:6 Oba 1:1 Zec 1:15.
paragraphs.anchor: For they persecute him whom thou hast smitten

paragraphs.text: Narrationes contexunt, they frame discourses to the grief of thy wounded ones, pouring into their wounds not oil, or balsam, but vinegar, or salt water, Heb. they number, or cipher up the grief; that is, saith one, they study and devise new ways of torturing them, so that he who would speak of them all, must keep a remembrance of their number.
paragraphs.anchor: And they talk to the grief of those whom thou hast wounded

paragraphs.text: Punish one sin with another (by giving them up to a reprobate sense, to an incurable hardness), and plague them soundly for their sin. The same Hebrew word signifieth both sin and punishment; these two are tied together with chains of adamant.
paragraphs.anchor: Add iniquity unto their iniquity

paragraphs.text: i.e. Hold them not righteous, nor bestow upon them thy crown of righteousness.
paragraphs.anchor: And let them not come into thy righteousness

paragraphs.text: Wherein they were never indeed written among those living in Jerusalem, Isa 4:3, those firstborn whose names are written in heaven, Heb 12:23, but they accounted themselves of that number, and were so esteemed by others. This was a mistake, and the psalmist prayeth God to make it appear so, Ne videantur in albun tuorum relati quibus verae vitro donum destinasti.
paragraphs.anchor: Let them be blotted out, &c.

paragraphs.text: The Church is usually so, and may sing, as here, Vaani gnani, &c., but her comfort is, 1. That Christ saith unto her, as Rev 2:9, I know thy sorrow and poverty (but that is nothing), thou art rich. 2. That her poverty is not penal, but medicinal; God’s dispensation to fit her for better riches; as a wise physician purgeth a foul hody till he bring it almost to skin and bone; but why? that, having made it poor, there may be a spring of better blood and spirits.
paragraphs.anchor: But I am poor and sorrowful

paragraphs.text: i.e. Agnitmn Deum. I will thankfully agnize and recognize God’s great goodness to me in this deliverance, with mine uttermost zeal and skill.
paragraphs.anchor: I will praise the name of God

paragraphs.text: True thankfulness is opimum et optimum saerificium, those calves of our lips, Hos 14:3 Heb 12:15. These calves or bullocks (as in the text) must, 1. Have horns and hoofs, be young and tender, the very best, of the best. 2. They must be slain; our thanks must proceed from a mortified mind. 3. They must be sacrificed; where is required, (1.) An altar, our praises must be tendered in the mediation of Christ. (2.) Fire, our hearts must be inflamed with zeal and ardency. (3.) Our hands must be laid on the head of the bullock; that is, we must in all humility confess our unworthiness, &c. This will surely please the Lord better than an ox or bullock that hath horns and hoofs.
paragraphs.anchor: This also shall please the Lord better, &c.

paragraphs.text: David’s great care was for others’ confirmation and comfort; much more Christ’s, witness that holy prayer of his, Joh 17:9
paragraphs.anchor: The humble shall see this and be glad

paragraphs.text: Which before was all lifeless. Pray that ye may joy. David did so often, Psa 6:1-10, &c.
paragraphs.anchor: Your heart shall live

paragraphs.text: He is the poor man’s king, the wronged man’s refuge; Trajan the emperor is renowned for this, that when he was mounted for a battle, he alighted again to bear the complaint of a poor woman that cried unto him for justice (Aeli. Spart.); and our Edward VI for this, that he would appoint certain hours to sit with the master of the requests, only to despatch the causes of the poor. God is much more to be magnified.
paragraphs.anchor: For the Lord heareth the poor

paragraphs.text: As they do in their kind; and have good cause so to do for their restoration by Christ, Rom 8:21.
paragraphs.anchor: Let the heaven and earth praise him

paragraphs.text: i.e. The Church universal.
paragraphs.anchor: For God will save Zion

paragraphs.text: The particular Churches.
paragraphs.anchor: And will build the cities

paragraphs.text: viz. The seed of his servants, Psa 69:36.
paragraphs.anchor: That they may dwell there

paragraphs.text: The faithful and their posterity after them shall be incorporated into the Church, and partake of all good things to all perpetuity.
paragraphs.anchor: The seed also of his servants shall inherit
